newsitem.title: UK: Major pleads with Protestants to maintain truce.
newsitem.headline: Major pleads with Protestants to maintain truce.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Sunday issued an emotional appeal to Protestant guerrillas contemplating an end to their Northern Ireland ceasefire -- "Don't, Don't, Don't."
Major warned the pro-British extremists that they would falling into a trap set for them by the Irish Republican Army, which is fighting to oust Britain from the troubled province.
"The IRA are isolated. Leave them isolated," Major said in a BBC Television interview.
Appealing directly to Protestant extremists, he said: "Don't, Don't Don't. If they do, then I fear you would back into full-scale violence."
Major's fervent appeal followed a warning on Saturday by a "senior Loyalist paramilitary source."

The source told the Irish Times that the outlawed Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) would end its two-year-old truce and launch a campaign against their pro-Irish nationalist adversaries if the IRA killed anyone.
The UFF is one of two Loyalist groups which called a ceasefire in October 1994 to match one declared and later abandoned by the IRA.

Urging restraint, Major said: "If the Loyalists were to return to violence as well, they would give the IRA the excuse they are longing for to move into greater violence and return to the days that we are still trying to get rid of."
"My advice to the Loyalists would be Don't. It is a trap, it is exactly what the IRA would most wish you to do," he added.

Northern Ireland's faltering peace talks have become bogged down in a stalemate and now there are fears that the whole process will be put on hold in the runup to the British general election that is due by May.

But Major, who has invested a large amount of political capital in trying to solve one of the most intractable guerrilla conflicts of the 20th century, said he hoped the process would not be put on hold.
"It is like playing multidimensional chess. Almost everybody can block it if they choose to block it. I would like to make progress. I would hope everybody else would like to make progress," he said.
But the New Year prospects for peace look gloomy with the IRA planting a huge bomb at Belfast Castle on New Year's Eve which was only abandoned because of intense security force activity.
Police said the 1,000 pound (500 kg) bomb had been designed for "mass murder".
The UFF warned that if that bomb had killed anyone, then its guerrillas "would be back, big time".
